title: Bounded result JSON retains host compatibility and projection responsibilities
observed_need: Expose a stable result document to mncs-actions and future Forge without losing typed native values or structured diagnostics.
current_language_behavior: Native assertions, suite verdicts, retained execution values, process-outcome classification, subprocess-fallback execution adjudication, the family-check path CheckResult policy projection, bounded run_id plus per-test lineage digests, per-test canonical execution/observation JSON construction for ordinary bounded string/null fields, bounded ArtifactStore payload/file digests, and public result JSON formatting for bounded JSON value trees are MNCS-owned. The public serializer sorts object keys, escapes and indents values, and emits the trailing newline. Documents through 16,300 bytes use the single-call application; documents through 32,684 bytes use 8,192-byte continuation windows, with the window application carrying native SHA-256 state across pages. Python still projects typed runtime values and raw diagnostics, reassembles bounded native pages, writes files, constructs canonical run_id JSON, supervises processes, and retains compatibility serialization/hash paths outside native bounds; the Rust bootstrap CLI retains its JSON and artifact boundaries.
why_insufficient: The bounded public serializer accepts at most 512 values, depth 63, 64 children per object, 256-byte keys, 1,024-byte scalar text, and 32,684 output bytes. Larger or unsupported values retain the compatibility path. Python still performs typed value projection, reassembles native UTF-8-safe pages, and writes public documents. The complete cross-repository evidence protocol and run_id JSON construction remain outside the native application surface. Native digest work is bounded by the toolchain 8,000,000-step ceiling per call; larger file/provenance hashes remain streamed through the host boundary. The Rust bootstrap CLI retains its JSON and artifact boundaries.
minimal_reproducer: tools/mncs_test.py::_public_result_json_payload receives a result requiring more than 16,300 output bytes, projects its JSON value tree, invokes test-public-result-json-window in continuation pages, and carries SHA-256 state through the window application. tests/test_public_result_json.py::test_native_json_supports_results_larger_than_legacy_window compares the emitted bytes and digest to independent Python JSON and SHA-256 results, including a UTF-8 scalar at an output chunk boundary. Python still constructs canonical run_id JSON for test-result-identity; test-lineage-identity builds ordinary per-test execution/observation JSON from bounded fields. Out-of-contract values retain exact compact-JSON compatibility behavior.
desired_direction: Extend the bounded native serializer and streaming identity capabilities through real consumers, while moving common text, collection, and typed-value projection mechanisms into reusable MNCS stdlib interfaces where migration requirements support them. Keep application policy and platform filesystem/process access at their existing ownership boundaries.
workaround: The MNCS test-check-result-projection application owns CheckResult policy and reference construction; test-lineage-identity constructs and hashes ordinary per-test execution/observation JSON; test-result-identity computes bounded run_id and ArtifactStore digests; test-public-result-json serializes small bounded results, and test-public-result-json-window serializes larger bounded values while carrying SHA-256 state across pages through mncs.std.sha256.v1. The adapter respects native row, field, payload, page, byte, and step limits, retains compatibility behavior outside them, and independently checks the final public-document digest. Python still constructs canonical run_id JSON, projects typed values, reassembles unresolved-message and JSON pages, performs filesystem access, and serializes unsupported or over-bound public values. It also retains process supervision, raw diagnostic transport, and explicit Actions/compatibility transport; it no longer classifies subprocess transport or decoded execution outcomes.
